title: IB Biology Exam Technique for November
summary: IB Biology exam technique for November: master Paper 1 and Paper 2 timing, command terms, data questions and extended responses in three weeks.
body_markdown:
November can feel like a distant exam session until it suddenly becomes a calendar of very few remaining days. For an IB Biology student with three weeks left, the answer is not to reread everything. It is to learn how the examination converts biological understanding into marks.


Effective **IB Biology exam technique** has three parts: knowing each paper’s structure, recognizing what the command term requires, and completing enough timed practice to make those decisions under pressure. The current course, first assessed in 2025, has two external examination papers. Paper 1 combines multiple-choice and data-based questions, while Paper 2 combines data analysis, short answers and extended responses.


Here is the three-week plan at a glance:


- **Week three:** diagnose weak topics and learn the papers.
- **Week two:** practise question types and review markscheme language.
- **Final week:** complete timed papers in Exam mode and repair recurring errors.
- **Every session:** record why marks were lost, not merely how many.


### First, know what November will ask of you


The current IB Biology assessment model is the same for May and November sessions. According to the current IB subject brief, external assessment contributes 80% of the final subject result. The remaining 20% comes from the scientific investigation.


Assessment SL HL Final weighting


Paper 1 1 hour 30 minutes 2 hours 36%


Paper 2 1 hour 30 minutes 2 hours 30 minutes 44%


Scientific investigation Internally assessed Internally assessed 20%


Paper 1A contains multiple-choice questions. Paper 1B contains syllabus-related data-based questions addressing the course themes. Paper 2 contains data-based questions, short-answer questions and extended-response questions.


These distinctions matter because knowledge behaves differently in each setting. A definition may be enough for one mark. A conclusion requires evidence from the supplied results. An extended response rewards an organized chain of relevant biology rather than everything you happen to remember.


Use RevisionDojo’s[IB Biology Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/questionbank/ib/biology) to separate practice by topic and difficulty. Pair it with[IB Biology Study Notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-biology) when an error exposes a genuine content gap.


### Three weeks before: build a diagnostic map


Imagine the student beginning on Monday with a familiar instinct: start at the first page of the notes and move forward. It feels orderly, but it hides the most useful information. They do not yet know which mistakes will cost them marks.


A better first step is a mixed, timed set from the Questionbank. After marking it, classify every lost mark:


- **Knowledge:** the biological fact or process was missing.
- **Interpretation:** the graph, table or experimental setup was misread.
- **Command term:** the response did not perform the requested task.
- **Precision:** wording was vague, incomplete or biologically inaccurate.
- **Timing:** the answer was rushed or left unfinished.


This turns a score into a plan. If most errors concern data interpretation, another evening of highlighting notes will not solve the problem. If terminology is weak,[IB Biology Flashcards](https://www.revisiondojo.com/flashcards) can make short retrieval sessions more useful than passive review. When an explanation still feels unclear, RevisionDojo’s[Jojo AI Chat](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ai) can help unpack the reasoning, but the final test should always be whether you can reconstruct the answer independently.


### IB Biology exam technique for Paper 1A


Paper 1A rewards accurate decisions at speed. Multiple-choice questions can test recall, application, calculations, diagrams and experimental reasoning. Treat each option as a claim to evaluate, not as a phrase that merely looks familiar.


Use this method:


1. Read the stem before studying the options.
2. Identify qualifiers such as *most likely* , *directly* or *only* .
3. Predict the answer where possible.
4. Eliminate options using a specific biological reason.
5. Mark uncertainty and move on rather than sacrificing several minutes.


For calculations, write a compact working line even if the response sheet records only an option. Check units, powers of ten and whether the question asks for a percentage change, ratio or raw difference. Estimation can expose an impossible choice before detailed arithmetic begins.


Do not repeatedly change an answer because it feels uncomfortable. Change it only when you identify a concrete error in your first reasoning. Uncertainty is normal; unsupported second-guessing is not a strategy.


A biology student asks a plant for revision advice while the plant recommends becoming a producer


### Paper 1B: let the data control the answer


Paper 1B is where many sensible students overuse memorized knowledge. A graph asks what the evidence shows, but the student answers with everything they know about enzymes or ecosystems.


Begin by orienting yourself:


- Read the title, axes, units and legend.
- Identify the independent and dependent variables.
- Notice controls, sample sizes, uncertainty indicators and anomalous points.
- Separate an observed pattern from a biological explanation.


For **identify** or **state** , give the requested feature directly. For **compare** , refer to both groups and use comparative language. For **calculate** , show substitution and retain suitable units. For **suggest** , propose a biologically plausible explanation supported by the information provided.


When describing a trend, quantify it. “The rate increased” is weaker than stating that it rose between two values across a specified interval. When evaluating a conclusion, discuss whether the evidence supports it, then consider limitations such as restricted range, uncontrolled variables, small samples or substantial variability. Do not invent flaws that the setup does not justify.


### Two weeks before: learn how Paper 2 awards marks


By week two, the student’s notebook should look less like a summary of Biology and more like a record of decisions. Paper 2 makes those decisions visible because it mixes concise responses with longer explanations.


Short-answer marks are usually attached to distinct valid points. If a question is worth three marks, one beautifully written idea is unlikely to be enough. Aim for three separate, relevant elements unless the task clearly requires a calculation or developed explanation.


Command terms set the depth:


- **State:** provide a brief answer without explanation.
- **Describe:** give a detailed account of features, patterns or events.
- **Explain:** connect causes and effects using biological reasoning.
- **Distinguish:** make the differences between two concepts clear.
- **Evaluate:** weigh evidence, strengths and limitations before reaching a judgment.


For extended responses, spend a brief moment planning. List the processes or claims you need, arrange them logically, and then write focused paragraphs. Use precise terms such as concentration gradient, active transport, allele frequency or competitive inhibition when they are genuinely relevant. Avoid introductions that simply repeat the question.


A strong explanation forms a chain: condition, mechanism and consequence. For example, do not stop at saying that temperature affects enzyme activity. Explain how increasing temperature changes molecular kinetic energy and collision frequency, then identify the point at which disruption of molecular interactions alters the active site and reduces activity.


RevisionDojo’s[AI grading tools](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grading) can help identify omissions in written work. Compare that feedback with the official markscheme logic and rewrite the answer from memory. Reading feedback feels productive; producing a better second answer is what changes performance.


### The final week: rehearse the whole experience


The last week before the **IB Biology November exams** should become increasingly exam-shaped. Complete full timed practice in RevisionDojo’s[Exam mode](https://www.revisiondojo.com/exams) , including[IB Biology Predicted Papers](https://www.revisiondojo.com/predicted-papers) and[Mock Exams](https://www.revisiondojo.com/mock-exams) .


Practise at the same time of day as the scheduled examination when practical. Use only the materials permitted for the real paper, remove notifications and continue through uncertainty. The purpose is not to create a comforting score. It is to expose what happens when concentration fades and the clock becomes visible.


Use marks to guide time. Avoid spending five minutes polishing a one-mark response while a longer question remains untouched. If stuck, write what can be justified, leave space and return later. Reserve a final check for missing units, unanswered subparts and responses that contradict the data.


After each timed paper, choose only three priorities for the next session. Ten vague weaknesses produce panic. Three specific repairs produce work.


### The final lesson is precision


Good **IB Biology exam tips** often sound simple: read carefully, use the data and watch the time. Their value appears through repetition. Under pressure, students fall back on habits, not intentions.


In the final three weeks, make those habits visible. Practise targeted questions in the RevisionDojo Questionbank, repair understanding with Study Notes and Flashcards, and then sit complete timed papers in Exam mode. RevisionDojo brings those tools together with AI Chat, grading support, Predicted Papers, Mock Exams, a Coursework Library and Tutors, making it the ultimate IB resource from first diagnosis to final rehearsal.


The goal is not to know every sentence ever written about Biology. It is to recognize the task, select the relevant science and communicate it precisely before time runs out.
